title: Food That Shaped the World · Episode 1

Rice: the grain that feeds billions
The potato: from the Andes to everywhere
Why chillies burn: the science of heat

units.t: Food That Shaped the World. Episode one.
In this episode: Salt: the rock that built civilisations, Rice: the grain that feeds billions, The potato: from the Andes to everywhere and Why chillies burn: the science of heat.
Part one. Salt: the rock that built civilisations.
Empires taxed it, armies guarded it and whole cities grew rich on it.
The humble white crystal on your table has one of the biggest stories in food.
The mineral we crave.
Salt is mostly sodium chloride, and sodium is essential.
Your nerves use it to fire signals, your muscles need it to contract, and your kidneys use it to manage the water in your body.
Hunter-gatherers who ate plenty of meat got enough from their food, but once people farmed grain, they needed extra.
Animals feel the same pull, and grazing animals wear tracks to natural salt licks.
Many ancient roads and settlements grew up along such routes.
Today the problem has flipped.
Most Australians eat more salt than health authorities recommend, and much of it is hidden in bread, sauces and processed meats.
Mines, springs and wells.
There are three classic sources.
Rock salt is mined from ancient seas that dried out and were buried.
At Hallstatt in the Austrian Alps, people have mined it since the Bronze Age, and the region grew rich enough that an early European culture is named after it.
Brine from salty springs is boiled down, as across Europe and China.
Sea water is dried by sun and wind in shallow ponds.
Australia is a major producer this way, with huge salt fields near Dampier in Western Australia, mostly shipped to Asia for industry.
In Sichuan, workers drilled narrow wells with heavy bits on bamboo cables.
In 1835 the Shenhai well at Zigong passed 1,000 metres, and natural gas from such wells fuelled the fires that boiled the brine.
Salt, tax and power.
Salt was big business for the state.

Under the Han dynasty in the 110s BC, China's government took control of salt and iron production, and a court debate in 81 BC, recorded as the Discourses on Salt and Iron, argued whether the state should profit from necessities.
A salt tax is hard to dodge.
France's gabelle was uneven, some regions paying many times more than others.
Smugglers were punished harshly, and the gabelle was one grievance of the French Revolution, abolished in 1790.
In 1930, Gandhi walked to the sea at Dandi and picked up natural salt in defiance of the British Indian salt monopoly.
The word salary comes from the Latin salarium, related to sal, meaning salt.
But there is no clear evidence that Roman soldiers were paid in salt.
Salt as a preserver.
Before refrigeration, salt was a main way to stop food rotting.
It works through osmosis.
Salt pulls water out of the food's cells and out of any bacteria, and the water left is so tightly bound to dissolved salt that most microbes cannot use it.
That is how salted cod, cured ham, anchovies and corned beef were made.
Salt cod became a huge international trade and is still loved in Portugal, Spain and the Caribbean.
Salt also steers fermentation.
In sauerkraut, kimchi and pickles, the right amount holds back spoilage organisms while helpful lactic acid bacteria do their sour, flavourful work.
Flakes, rocks and iodine.
Sea salt, rock salt, pink Himalayan salt and table salt are overwhelmingly sodium chloride.
Trace minerals tint some salts, but in the amounts you eat they make little nutritional difference.
What changes is the crystal.
Big flakes dissolve slowly and crunch on top of food, while fine salt packs densely, so a teaspoon of fine salt is noticeably saltier than a teaspoon of flakes.
That is why a recipe calling for a teaspoon of salt can come out differently.
Iodine is the other difference.
Deficiency can cause goitre and affect brain development, so many countries add iodine to salt.
Since 2009, Australian bakers have been required to use iodised salt in most bread, a quiet public health measure.
The key idea: Our bodies need sodium for nerves, muscles and water balance, which is why people and animals have always sought out salt.
Part two. Rice: the grain that feeds billions.
Billions of people eat rice every day.
Its story runs from ancient Chinese wetlands to a ‘miracle rice’ and paddies in the New South Wales Riverina.
Two origins, flooded fields.
Most rice is Asian rice, Oryza sativa, domesticated in the Yangtze region of China roughly 9,000 years ago, though researchers still debate how japonica and indica arose.
Farmers selected plants whose grains stayed on the stalk, easing harvest.
Separately, West Africans domesticated African rice, Oryza glaberrima, in the Niger River delta around 3,000 years ago.
It is hardy and still grown, though Asian rice has largely replaced it.
Rice does not need to be underwater, but it tolerates flooding because air channels carry oxygen to its roots.
Weeds struggle in flooded soil, so farmers flood paddies to control them.
The downside is methane from microbes in flooded soil, which farmers try to cut by alternate wetting and drying.
Sticky or fluffy.
Rice starch comes in two forms.
Amylose is a straight chain, and rices high in it, such as many long-grain varieties, cook up firm with separate grains.
Amylopectin is highly branched and makes rice soft and sticky.
Japanese short-grain rice has relatively little amylose, so it clumps nicely for sushi.
Risotto rices such as arborio release creamy starch when stirred.
Sticky or glutinous rice, used in Thai and Lao cooking, is almost entirely amylopectin and contains no gluten; glutinous means glue-like.
Jasmine tends to be softer and stickier than basmati.
Rinsing removes surface starch and gives looser grains.
There are two classic methods: absorption, where grains soak up a measured amount of water, and boiling in plenty of water that is drained.
White rice and vitamins.
Brown rice keeps its bran and germ, which hold fibre, oils, minerals and B vitamins.
White rice has them polished away, so it cooks faster and lasts longer but is less nutritious.
As steam-powered mills spread polished rice across Asia in the late nineteenth century, beriberi became widespread, causing nerve damage, weakness and heart failure.
In the Dutch East Indies, now Indonesia, the physician Christiaan Eijkman noticed in the 1890s that chickens fed polished rice developed similar symptoms and recovered on unpolished rice.
His work helped show that tiny amounts of certain substances in food are essential.
The missing substance proved to be thiamine, vitamin B1, and Eijkman shared the 1929 Nobel Prize.
Miracle rice, thirsty crops.
In the 1960s, experts feared mass famine in Asia as populations outgrew harvests.
At the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines, breeders crossed a tall Indonesian variety with a Taiwanese dwarf.
The result, IR8, released in 1966, had short, stiff stems.
Tall varieties fell over under heavy fertiliser, but IR8 carried heavy heads of grain and often yielded far more.
Known as "miracle rice", it was central to the Green Revolution.
The costs included heavier use of fertiliser, pesticides and water, and the loss of many traditional varieties.
Australia has grown rice commercially for about a century, mainly in the Riverina, on Murrumbidgee and Murray water.
Growers achieve some of the world's highest yields, but the crop swings with drought, collapsing in very dry years.
Leftover rice safety.
Rice can carry spores of Bacillus cereus, which survive cooking.
If cooked rice sits warm for hours, the spores grow and make toxins that reheating will not destroy, causing vomiting.
So cool leftover rice quickly, refrigerate it within an hour or so, eat it within a day or so and reheat it until steaming hot.
Spreading rice on a tray helps it cool faster.
The risk comes from the time the rice spends warm, not from the rice itself, which is a safe, healthy staple for billions of people when handled sensibly.
The key idea: Asian and African rice were domesticated separately, and flooding paddies helps rice outcompete weeds.
Part three. The potato: from the Andes to everywhere.
A knobbly tuber from the high Andes fed empires, sparked suspicion in Europe, and became one of the world's most important foods.
Born in the Andes.
The potato we eat was domesticated in the Andes, near Lake Titicaca in southern Peru and northern Bolivia, perhaps 7,000 to 10,000 years ago.
Farmers grew food above 3,000 metres, with frost, thin air and short seasons.
They bred thousands of varieties, from purple and red to gold and near black, each suited to particular soils, heights and uses.
The International Potato Center in Lima keeps a huge collection as insurance for the future.
Fresh potatoes rot, so Andean peoples invented chuño.
Potatoes freeze overnight on the ground, thaw in the sun and are trodden to squeeze out water.
The light, hard result lasts for years, and the Inca state stored it in roadside warehouses.
Arriving in Europe.
Spanish soldiers met the potato in the 1530s, and by the 1560s and 1570s it had crossed the Atlantic.
Europeans were wary.
It belongs to the nightshade family, and its leaves and green parts really do contain toxic glycoalkaloids, including solanine.
Gradually farmers noticed that potatoes gave far more calories per hectare than wheat or rye, grew in poor soil and cool climates, and could stay in the ground until needed.
In France, the army pharmacist Antoine-Augustin Parmentier had survived on potatoes as a prisoner of war.
He promoted them tirelessly, and in 1772 the Paris Faculty of Medicine declared them fit to eat.
A story says he guarded a potato field by day but not by night, so locals would steal it.
That tale may be embellished.
Ireland's Great Famine.
By the 1840s, much of Ireland's rural poor relied on potatoes for most of their food.
Many grew a single high-yielding variety, the Lumper, so the crop was genetically very uniform.
In 1845 late blight, caused by the fungus-like Phytophthora infestans, turned potatoes black and rotten in the ground, and it returned in following years.
Roughly a million people died of starvation and disease, and more than a million emigrated, many to North America, Britain and Australia.
Political choices made it worse: food continued to be exported from Ireland, and relief was inadequate.
The famine is a lasting lesson about the danger of depending on a single crop.
A global staple.
The potato spread across Europe, Asia and Africa, and is now one of the most important food crops on Earth.
As of the mid-2020s, China grows the most, followed by India.
Potatoes give more food per hectare than most grains and need less water, which matters as populations grow and the climate changes.
They are also more nutritious than their reputation.
A potato provides energy as starch, along with fibre, potassium and a useful amount of vitamin C, with much of the fibre in the skin.
It is usually what we do to potatoes, such as deep frying and adding salt, butter and cream, that makes them less healthy, not the potato itself.
Cooking and storing them.
Potatoes fall into two camps.
Floury or starchy varieties, such as russets, break apart when cooked and suit fluffy mash, roasts and chips.
Waxy varieties, such as kipflers and small new potatoes, hold their shape for salads and boiling.
The difference comes from starch content and how the cells hold together.
Store potatoes somewhere cool, dark and dry.
Light turns them green as they make chlorophyll, and alongside it they can make more glycoalkaloids, which taste bitter and can cause illness in large amounts.
Cut away green patches and sprouts generously, and throw out potatoes that are very green or taste bitter.
Keeping them out of the light is the simplest fix.
The key idea: The potato was domesticated in the high Andes, and Andean peoples developed thousands of varieties and a way to store it for years.
Part four. Why chillies burn: the science of heat.
Chilli heat is not a taste at all.
It is a clever chemical trick that fools your pain sensors, and the story of how it conquered the world's kitchens is just as surprising.
From Mexico to the world.
Thai, Indian, Sichuan and Korean food all learned to use chillies only in the last five centuries.
Chillies, plants of the genus Capsicum, originated in the Americas and were domesticated in Mexico thousands of years ago.
After Columbus's voyages, Spanish and especially Portuguese traders carried them around the world.
Unlike many crops, they were easy to grow from seed, thrived in warm climates and offered a cheap, intense flavour.
Within about a century they grew in India, Africa and South-East Asia, where local cooks made them their own, often replacing or supplementing black pepper.
How capsaicin fools you.
The burn comes mainly from capsaicinoids, chiefly capsaicin.
Taste buds do not detect it.
Instead it binds to TRPV1, a protein on pain-sensing nerve endings.
TRPV1 normally detects dangerous heat, switching on above roughly 43 degrees Celsius.
Capsaicin flips the same switch, so your brain concludes your mouth is burning though the temperature has not changed.
That is why chilli can make you sweat and flush.
Work on how such receptors sense temperature and pain earned David Julius a share of the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
In 1912 pharmacist Wilbur Scoville measured heat by diluting extract until tasters felt none.
Labs now measure capsaicinoids directly and convert to Scoville units.
A bell pepper scores zero, a jalapeno a few thousand, and the hottest bred varieties exceed two million.
Why plants burn us.
Why would a plant make something that burns?
One explanation is directed deterrence.
Mammals chewing chillies crush the seeds, while birds swallow them whole and spread them in droppings.
Birds' TRPV1 is insensitive to capsaicin, so they eat the hottest chillies in comfort.
Capsaicin may also protect fruit from fungi: wild chillies in wetter parts of Bolivia, where fungal attack is more common, tend to be hotter.
Scientists still debate how much each factor matters.
Humans are among very few animals that seek out the burn.
Psychologist Paul Rozin calls it benign masochism, like enjoying a roller coaster while your brain knows you are safe.
Endorphins may add pleasure, though how much is uncertain.
Tolerance builds, since repeated exposure makes nerve endings less responsive for a while.
Where the heat hides.
Many people think the seeds are the hottest part.
In fact capsaicin is made mostly in the pale, spongy ribs, or placenta, that hold the seeds.
Seeds taste hot because they press against it.
Removing the ribs and seeds tames a chilli considerably.
Capsaicin is oily.
It dissolves poorly in water but well in fats and alcohol, so gulping water mostly spreads it around.
Dairy such as milk and yoghurt helps, probably because its fat and a protein called casein help carry capsaicin away.
Starchy foods like rice or bread can also give some relief by mopping up the oil.
Handle very hot chillies with gloves, avoid touching your eyes, and take extreme chilli challenges cautiously.
Capsaicin is also the active ingredient in some pain-relief creams and in pepper spray.
Other kinds of fire.
Not every pungent spice works like chilli.
Black pepper gets its bite from piperine, which also activates TRPV1 and a related receptor, though more mildly.
Wasabi, horseradish and mustard rely on isothiocyanates, which are volatile, so the heat rushes up the nose and fades quickly.
They activate a different receptor, TRPA1, which also responds to irritants such as the fumes from cut onions.
Sichuan pepper, from the dried husks of a prickly ash shrub unrelated to chillies or black pepper, does something stranger.
A compound called hydroxy-alpha-sanshool produces a tingling, buzzing numbness that researchers have compared to a mild vibration on the lips.
Sichuan cooking pairs this numbing sensation with chilli heat in mala, meaning 'numbing and spicy'.
The key idea: Chillies are American plants that spread around the globe within a century of Columbus's voyages.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why did early farmers need extra salt that hunter-gatherers often did not?
Answer. Grain supplies little sodium, unlike a meat-rich diet.
Question two. Why do rice paddies work well as flooded fields?
Answer. Weeds struggle in flooded soil, but rice tolerates it.
Question three. Why did Andean peoples invent chuño?
Answer. Fresh potatoes rot, so they needed long-term storage.
Question four. Why did chillies spread so quickly after 1492?
Answer. They were easy to grow and full of flavour.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
